claim: Faithful segregation of bacterial chromosomes relies on the ParABS partitioning system and the SMC complex.
source: Faithful segregation of bacterial chromosomes relies on the ParABS partitioning system and the SMC complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Britton et al., 1998; Ireton et al., 1994; Jensen and Shapiro, 1999; Marbouty et al., 2015; Mohl and Gober, 1997; Song and Loparo, 2015; Wang et al., 2014).

claim: The ParABS system consists of the ATPase protein ParA, the DNA-binding protein ParB, and a centromere-like palindromic DNA sequence named parS.
source: The ParABS system consists of the ATPase protein ParA, the DNA-binding protein ParB, and a centromere-like palindromic DNA sequence named parS (Funnell, 2016; Lin and Grossman, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Funnell, 2016; Lin and Grossman, 1998).

claim: Multiple ParB proteins co-localize with SMC complexes at a given parS site forming distinctive clusters in the cell in Bacillus subtilis.
source: In vivo imaging experiments in Bacillus subtilis showed that multiple ParB proteins co-localize with SMC complexes at a given parS site forming distinctive clusters in the cell (Gruber and Errington, 2009; Minnen et al., 2011; Sullivan et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior in vivo imaging experiments (Gruber and Errington, 2009; Minnen et al., 2011; Sullivan et al., 2009).

claim: ParB covers regions of up to 18 kilobase pairs (kbp) of DNA surrounding parS according to chromatin immuno-precipitation (ChIP) experiments.
source: Notably, chromatin immuno-precipitation (ChIP) experiments indicate that ParB covers regions of up to 18 kilobase pairs (kbp) of DNA surrounding parS (Breier and Grossman, 2007; Graham et al., 2014; Minnen et al., 2016; Murray et al., 2006; Rodionov et al., 1999), a phenomenon named spreading.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to ChIP experiments (Breier and Grossman, 2007; Graham et al., 2014; Minnen et al., 2016; Murray et al., 2006; Rodionov et al., 1999).

claim: ParB spreading was originally interpreted as the formation of a nucleoprotein filament extending from a parS nucleation site.
source: Originally, this spreading was interpreted as the formation of a nucleoprotein filament extending from a parS nucleation site (Murray et al., 2006; Rodionov et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior interpretations (Murray et al., 2006; Rodionov et al., 1999).

claim: ParB foci contained far too few proteins to coat tens of kbp-long DNA segments.
source: However, it later became clear that ParB foci contained far too few proteins to coat tens of kbp-long DNA segments (Graham et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Graham et al., 2014).

claim: ParB can self-associate to form networks which include specific binding to parS sequences but also non-specific binding to distal DNA segments.
source: Instead, we and others have shown that ParB can self-associate to form networks which include specific binding to parS sequences but also non-specific binding to distal DNA segments.
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' own work and citations to others' work.

claim: ParB self-association results in the condensation and bridging of DNA at low forces (below 1 pN).
source: Overall, this results in the condensation and bridging of DNA at low forces (below 1 pN) (Fisher et al., 2017; Graham et al., 2014; Madariaga-Marcos et al., 2019; Madariaga-Marcos et al., 2018; Taylor et al., 2015), and could explain how distant regions of DNA are bound by limited numbers of ParB proteins as shown in ChIP experiments.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Fisher et al., 2017; Graham et al., 2014; Madariaga-Marcos et al., 2019; Madariaga-Marcos et al., 2018; Taylor et al., 2015).

claim: DNA condensation by ParB has only been observed in vitro at high ParB concentrations, in the low micromolar range.
source: However, DNA condensation has only been observed in vitro at high ParB concentrations, in the low micromolar range.
evidence: This claim is based on prior in vitro observations.

claim: parS sequences did not affect DNA condensation at high ParB concentrations.
source: Moreover, and unexpectedly, parS sequences did not affect DNA condensation under these conditions (Taylor et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Taylor et al., 2015).

claim: The N-terminal domain (NTD) of ParB binds ParA.
source: The N-terminal domain (NTD) binds ParA (Bouet and Funnell, 1999; Davis et al., 1992; Radnedge et al., 1998; Vecchiarelli et al., 2010) and was recently appreciated to contain a CTP-binding pocket that serves as a CTP-dependent dimerization interface (Osorio-Valeriano et al., 2019; Soh et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Bouet and Funnell, 1999; Davis et al., 1992; Radnedge et al., 1998; Vecchiarelli et al., 2010).

claim: The N-terminal domain (NTD) of ParB contains a CTP-binding pocket that serves as a CTP-dependent dimerization interface.
source: The N-terminal domain (NTD) binds ParA (Bouet and Funnell, 1999; Davis et al., 1992; Radnedge et al., 1998; Vecchiarelli et al., 2010) and was recently appreciated to contain a CTP-binding pocket that serves as a CTP-dependent dimerization interface (Osorio-Valeriano et al., 2019; Soh et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent work (Osorio-Valeriano et al., 2019; Soh et al., 2019).

claim: Mutation R80A in the CTP-binding pocket has been shown to impair nucleoid segregation and ParB spreading.
source: Mutation R80A in the CTP-binding pocket has been shown to impair nucleoid segregation and ParB spreading (Autret et al., 2001; Breier and Grossman, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Autret et al., 2001; Breier and Grossman, 2007).

claim: A central DNA-binding domain (CDBD) binds specifically to the palindromic parS sequence and may also facilitate dimerization.
source: A central DNA-binding domain (CDBD) binds specifically to the palindromic parS sequence and may also facilitate dimerization (Leonard et al., 2004; Schumacher and Funnell, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Leonard et al., 2004; Schumacher and Funnell, 2005).

claim: The mutation R149G within a helix-turn-helix motif impedes parS binding.
source: In this central region, the mutation R149G within a helix-turn-helix motif impedes parS binding (Autret et al., 2001; Fisher et al., 2017; Gruber and Errington, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Autret et al., 2001; Fisher et al., 2017; Gruber and Errington, 2009).

claim: The C-terminal domain (CTD) forms dimers with a lysine-rich surface that binds to DNA non-specifically.
source: Finally, the C-terminal domain (CTD) forms dimers with a lysine-rich surface that binds to DNA non-specifically (Fisher et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Fisher et al., 2017).

claim: Interactions between CTDs are essential for condensation in vitro and for the formation of ParB foci in vivo.
source: Interactions between CTDs are essential for condensation in vitro and for the formation of ParB foci in vivo (Fisher et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Fisher et al., 2017).

claim: ParB networks are highly dynamic and display a continual exchange of protein-protein and protein-DNA interfaces.
source: Further work using lateral pulling of long DNA molecules in a magnetic tweezers (MT) setup combined with total internal reflection fluorescence microscopy (TIRFM) demonstrated that ParB networks are highly dynamic and display a continual exchange of protein-protein and protein-DNA interfaces (Madariaga-Marcos et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Madariaga-Marcos et al., 2019).

claim: B. subtilis ParB and the Myxococcus xanthus ParB hydrolyse cytidine triphosphate (CTP) to cytidine diphosphate (CDP).
source: Recently, two laboratories demonstrated independent that B. subtilis ParB and the Myxococcus xanthus ParB hydrolyse cytidine triphosphate (CTP) to cytidine diphosphate (CDP) (Osorio-Valeriano et al., 2019; Soh et al., 2019) and require CTP for partition complex formation in vivo (Osorio-Valeriano et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent work (Osorio-Valeriano et al., 2019; Soh et al., 2019).

claim: ParB requires CTP for partition complex formation in vivo.
source: Recently, two laboratories demonstrated independent that B. subtilis ParB and the Myxococcus xanthus ParB hydrolyse cytidine triphosphate (CTP) to cytidine diphosphate (CDP) (Osorio-Valeriano et al., 2019; Soh et al., 2019) and require CTP for partition complex formation in vivo (Osorio-Valeriano et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to recent work (Osorio-Valeriano et al., 2019).

claim: parS DNA stimulates the binding and hydrolysis of CTP by ParB.
source: Importantly, parS DNA stimulates the binding and hydrolysis of CTP (Osorio-Valeriano et al., 2019; Soh et al., 2019), CTP has been shown to be necessary for ParB spreading in vitro (Jalal et al., 2020), and a model has been proposed in which centromeres assemble via the loading of ParB-DNA sliding clamps at parS sequences (Jalal et al., 2020; Soh et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent work (Osorio-Valeriano et al., 2019; Soh et al., 2019).

claim: CTP has been shown to be necessary for ParB spreading in vitro.
source: Importantly, parS DNA stimulates the binding and hydrolysis of CTP (Osorio-Valeriano et al., 2019; Soh et al., 2019), CTP has been shown to be necessary for ParB spreading in vitro (Jalal et al., 2020), and a model has been proposed in which centromeres assemble via the loading of ParB-DNA sliding clamps at parS sequences (Jalal et al., 2020; Soh et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to recent work (Jalal et al., 2020).

claim: A model has been proposed in which centromeres assemble via the loading of ParB-DNA sliding clamps at parS sequences.
source: Importantly, parS DNA stimulates the binding and hydrolysis of CTP (Osorio-Valeriano et al., 2019; Soh et al., 2019), CTP has been shown to be necessary for ParB spreading in vitro (Jalal et al., 2020), and a model has been proposed in which centromeres assemble via the loading of ParB-DNA sliding clamps at parS sequences (Jalal et al., 2020; Soh et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent work (Jalal et al., 2020; Soh et al., 2019).

claim: Binding of ParB around parS is enhanced by the presence of CTP or the non-hydrolysable analogue CTPγS.
source: Binding around parS is enhanced by the presence of CTP or the non-hydrolysable analogue CTPγS.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 1).

claim: ParB proteins are detected at a lower density in distal non-specific DNA.
source: However, ParB proteins are also detected at a lower density in distal non-specific DNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 1 and Figure 2).

claim: ParB detection in distal non-specific DNA requires the presence of a parS loading site.
source: This requires the presence of a parS loading site and is prevented by protein roadblocks, consistent with one-dimensional diffusion by a sliding clamp.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 2).

claim: ParB detection in distal non-specific DNA is prevented by protein roadblocks, consistent with one-dimensional diffusion by a sliding clamp.
source: This requires the presence of a parS loading site and is prevented by protein roadblocks, consistent with one-dimensional diffusion by a sliding clamp.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 2) and inference from the roadblock experiments.

claim: ParB diffusion on non-specific DNA is corroborated by direct visualization and quantification of movement of individual quantum dot labelled ParB.
source: ParB diffusion on non-specific DNA is corroborated by direct visualization and quantification of movement of individual quantum dot labelled ParB.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 3).

claim: The spreading activity has an absolute requirement for CTP binding but not hydrolysis.
source: Magnetic tweezers experiments show that the spreading activity, which has an absolute requirement for CTP binding but not hydrolysis, results in the condensation of parS-containing DNA molecules at low nanomolar protein concentrations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 4 and Figure 5).

claim: The spreading activity results in the condensation of parS-containing DNA molecules at low nanomolar protein concentrations.
source: Magnetic tweezers experiments show that the spreading activity, which has an absolute requirement for CTP binding but not hydrolysis, results in the condensation of parS-containing DNA molecules at low nanomolar protein concentrations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 4).

claim: ParB hydrolyses CTP in the absence of DNA at ~0.2 CTP molecules per dimer, per minute.
source: ParB hydrolyses cytidine triphosphate (CTP) in the absence of DNA at ~0.2 CTP molecules per dimer, per minute.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: CTP hydrolysis by ParB increases three- to four-fold in the presence of parS DNA.
source: CTP hydrolysis increases three- to four-fold in the presence of parS DNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Nucleotides ATP, CTPγS, GTP, or UTP cannot be hydrolysed by ParB.
source: Nucleotides ATP, CTPγS, GTP, or UTP cannot be hydrolysed by ParB.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The CTP hydrolysis rate by ParB increases linearly with the concentration of parS sequences.
source: The CTP hydrolysis rate increases linearly with the concentration of parS sequences.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ParBAF488 retains parS-stimulated CTPase activity within two-fold levels of wild-type protein.
source: ParBAF488 retains parS-stimulated CTPase activity within two-fold levels of wild-type protein, which is likely attributable to inactivation of a fraction of the protein by the long labelling procedure.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The presence of CTP enhanced the fluorescence intensity within the parS clusters by three- to four-fold compared to in the absence of CTP.
source: However, the presence of CTP enhanced the fluorescence intensity within the parS clusters by three- to four-fold compared to in the absence of CTP (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1F.

claim: The higher fluorescence intensity measured in the presence of CTP reflects a greater number of ParB molecules bound at or around the parS sequences compared to the no CTP condition.
source: Therefore, these images represent the steady-state occupancy of ParB on DNA and the higher fluorescence intensity measured in the CTP case reflects a greater number of ParB molecules bound at or around the parS sequences compared to the no CTP condition.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data and the understanding of the system.

claim: ParB binding to parS did not require CTP in agreement with previous EMSA and bio-layer interferometric analysis.
source: Importantly, ParB binding to parS did not require CTP in agreement with previous EMSA (Taylor et al., 2015) and bio-layer interferometric analysis (Jalal et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in the manuscript and citations to prior work (Taylor et al., 2015; Jalal et al., 2020).

claim: The 30 s average intensity profile clearly distinguished six foci corresponding to groups of ParB molecules precisely at their expected positions.
source: The 30 s average intensity profile clearly distinguished six foci corresponding to groups of ParB molecules precisely at their expected positions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 4C.

claim: The gradual decay of the fluorescence over tens of seconds indicates that the photobleaching kinetics are faster than the rates of ParB binding and unbinding.
source: The gradual decay of the fluorescence over tens of seconds (Figure 1—figure supplement 4D) indicates that the photobleaching kinetics are faster than the rates of ParB binding and unbinding.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 4D.

claim: ParB proteins were sparsely distributed along the entire non-specific region under CTP or CTPγS conditions.
source: Indeed, ParB proteins were sparsely distributed along the entire non-specific region (i.e., they did not only accumulate at or near the parS cluster) (red arrow, Figure 2B and Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2B and Figure 2C.

claim: The intensity in the non-parS region decayed within 1–2 s, an apparently shorter timescale than in the parS regions.
source: The intensity in this non-parS region decayed within 1–2 s, an apparently shorter timescale than in the parS regions (Animation 1), re-enforcing the idea that protein turnover is slow compared to photobleaching.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Animation 1.

claim: A control experiment using a non-parS DNA showed no protein bound at all in the presence of CTP.
source: Crucially, a control experiment using a non-parS DNA showed no protein bound at all in the presence of CTP (Figure 2B and C), supporting the notion that proteins located outside parS reached that location through the parS entry site.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Proteins located outside parS reached that location through the parS entry site.
source: Crucially, a control experiment using a non-parS DNA showed no protein bound at all in the presence of CTP (Figure 2B and C), supporting the notion that proteins located outside parS reached that location through the parS entry site.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the control experiment data.

claim: ParB spreading is hindered by DNA-binding protein 'roadblocks' engineered close to parS.
source: Previous in vitro and in vivo experiments have shown that ParB spreading is hindered by DNA-binding protein 'roadblocks' engineered close to parS (Murray et al., 2006; Rodionov and Yarmolinsky, 2004; Soh et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Murray et al., 2006; Rodionov and Yarmolinsky, 2004; Soh et al., 2019).

claim: EcoRIE111G roadblocks constrained ParB spreading.
source: Importantly, a faint region also appeared flanking the parS cluster and bordered by the EcoRIE111G roadblocks, which appeared to have constrained ParB spreading (see red arrows, Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2F.

claim: CTP binding promotes movement of ParB over kbp distances away from parS sites to non-specific regions of DNA.
source: Altogether, these experiments show that CTP binding promotes movement of ParB over kbp distances away from parS sites to non-specific regions of DNA.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in Figure 2.

claim: ParB movement occurs by sliding from parS.
source: The fact that this movement can be constrained by protein roadblocks suggests that it occurs by sliding from parS.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the roadblock experiments.

claim: The diffusion constant of ParB was 0.41±0.02 µm2 s−1 (mean±SEM, n=177) or 3.5±0.2 × 106 bp2 s−1.
source: The diffusion constant of ParB was 0.41±0.02 µm2 s−1 (mean±SEM, n=177) or 3.5±0.2 × 106 bp2 s−1, assuming a rise per base pair of 0.34 nm.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3.

claim: ParB proteins bound to parS remained mostly immobile.
source: In contrast, ParB proteins bound to parS remained mostly immobile (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3F.

claim: The ParB diffusion constant data are consistent with previous single-molecule experiments performed in the absence of CTP.
source: These data are consistent with previous single-molecule experiments performed in the absence of CTP (Graham et al., 2014) and with the recently calculated ParB diffusion constant of 0.7 µm2 s−1 using super-resolution microscopy (Guilhas et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Graham et al., 2014; Guilhas et al., 2020).

claim: Guilhas et al. reported a much lower value of 0.05 µm2 s−1 for ParB clustered in parS nucleoprotein condensates.
source: In addition, Guilhas et al. also reported a much lower value of 0.05 µm2 s−1 for ParB clustered in parS nucleoprotein condensates, which likely reflects our observation of immobile ParB proteins at parS (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Guilhas et al., 2020).

claim: The ParB diffusion constant obtained with CTPγS was 0.38±0.02 µm2 s−1 (mean±SEM, n=185).
source: The ParB diffusion constant obtained with CTPγS was 0.38±0.02 µm2 s−1 (mean±SEM, n=185).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the presence of CTP-Mg2+, ParB condensed parS-containing DNA at nanomolar concentrations.
source: In the presence of CTP-Mg2+, ParB condensed parS-containing DNA at nanomolar concentrations, much lower than those reported before (Fisher et al., 2017; Taylor et al., 2015; Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4.

claim: DNA condensation was observed at ParB concentrations of 5–10 nM, but the rate was markedly slower.
source: In fact, DNA condensation was observed at even lower concentrations of 5–10 nM, but the rate was markedly slower (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: DNA was condensed by ParB at forces of up to 1 pN using only 10 nM protein in the presence of CTP-Mg2+.
source: In the presence of CTP-Mg2+, DNA was condensed by ParB at forces of up to 1 pN using only 10 nM protein (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4D.

claim: Experiments using ATP, UTP, or GTP did not produce any DNA condensation, confirming the specificity of ParB for CTP.
source: Experiments using ATP, UTP, or GTP did not produce any DNA condensation, confirming the specificity of ParB for CTP and linking CTP binding to condensation (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4E.

claim: ParB did not induce any condensation in a buffer containing 1 mM EDTA and 200 nM ParB2.
source: ParB did not induce any condensation in a buffer containing 1 mM EDTA and 200 nM ParB2 (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4F.

claim: Mg2+ is a cofactor of CTP at the CTP-binding site.
source: The recent crystal structure of the M. xanthus ParB-like protein PadC showed that Mg2+ is a cofactor of CTP at the CTP-binding site (Osorio-Valeriano et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Osorio-Valeriano et al., 2019).

claim: CTP binding is abolished in BsParBR80A.
source: Additionally, CTP binding is also abolished in BsParBR80A (Soh et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Soh et al., 2019).

claim: MT experiments showed no DNA condensation by ParBR80A under CTP-Mg2+ conditions.
source: Indeed, MT experiments showed no DNA condensation by ParBR80A under CTP-Mg2+ conditions (Figure 4G) supporting the idea that CTP binding is required for condensation at nanomolar ParB concentrations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4G.

claim: In the absence of CTP, ParB was unable to condense parS-containing DNA unless its concentration was raised to the micromolar range.
source: In the absence of CTP, ParB was unable to condense parS-containing DNA unless its concentration was raised to the micromolar range, as reported previously (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C; Taylor et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C and a citation to prior work (Taylor et al., 2015).

claim: No significant difference in force-extension measurements was observed between CTP and CTPγS conditions.
source: We did not observe any significant difference in force-extension measurements compared to the CTP case (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5A compared to Figure 4D.

claim: DNA condensation by ParB and CTPγS was abolished by EDTA.
source: The DNA was still condensed at nanomolar ParB and condensation was abolished by EDTA (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5B.

claim: Experiments using CDP showed no DNA condensation under conditions proficient for condensation.
source: Additional experiments using CDP showed no DNA condensation under conditions proficient for condensation (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5C.

claim: Binding to both CTP and Mg2+ cofactor is required for DNA condensation by nanomolar ParB, but CTP hydrolysis is not.
source: Altogether, we conclude that binding to both CTP and Mg2+ cofactor is required for DNA condensation by nanomolar ParB, but that CTP hydrolysis is not.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Experiments using a DNA substrate with scrambled parS sequences did not show condensation even at ParB2 concentrations of 200 nM.
source: Experiments using a DNA substrate with scrambled parS sequences did not show condensation even at ParB2 concentrations of 200 nM (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6A.

claim: No condensation was observed using ParBR149G under conditions proficient for condensation with wild-type ParB.
source: As expected, no condensation was observed using ParBR149G under conditions proficient for condensation with wild-type ParB (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6B.

claim: DNA condensation was observed in substrates with 26, 13, and 7 parS sequences with a clear correlation between the number of parS and the maximum force permissive for condensation.
source: DNA condensation was observed in substrates with 26, 13, and 7 parS sequences with a clear correlation between the number of parS and the maximum force permissive for condensation (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6D.

claim: Experiments with substrates containing 1, 2, or 4 copies of parS did not result in condensation even at a relatively high ParB2 concentration of 200 nM.
source: Experiments with substrates containing 1, 2, or 4 copies of parS did not result in condensation even at a relatively high ParB2 concentration of 200 nM (Figure 6E and Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6E and Figure 6F.

claim: A single parS is sufficient for chromosome segregation and to promote ParB focus formation.
source: However, it has been reported that a single parS is sufficient for chromosome segregation and to promote ParB focus formation (Broedersz et al., 2014; Jecz et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Broedersz et al., 2014; Jecz et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2017).

claim: TPM and AFM experiments performed in the absence of force indicate that a single parS sequence is sufficient for DNA condensation under CTP-Mg2+ conditions.
source: Indeed, further experiments using TPM and AFM performed in the absence of force indicate that a single parS sequence is sufficient for DNA condensation under CTP-Mg2+ conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: CTP binding dramatically enhances DNA condensation by ParB such that it occurs efficiently at low nanomolar ParB concentration.
source: Together, these data show that CTP binding dramatically enhances DNA condensation by ParB such that it occurs efficiently at low nanomolar ParB concentration.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in Figures 4-6.

claim: The stimulatory effect of CTP on DNA condensation is completely specific for parS-containing DNA molecules.
source: Importantly, this stimulatory effect is completely specific for parS-containing DNA molecules as CTP does not improve the condensation of parS-free molecules that can be observed at high concentration of ParB.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in Figures 4-6.

claim: CTP binding to ParB induces a conformational change to a sliding clamp which then escapes from parS to neighbouring non-specific DNA.
source: (Step 2) CTP binding to ParB induces a conformational change to a sliding clamp which then escapes from parS to neighbouring non-specific DNA.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data and the proposed model in Figure 7.

claim: ParB spreading and diffusion promotes the interaction with other CTP-ParB dimers through the C-terminal domain (CTD) of ParB, resulting in DNA condensation by forming large DNA loops.
source: (Step 3) ParB spreading and diffusion promotes the interaction with other CTP-ParB dimers through the C-terminal domain (CTD) of ParB (Fisher et al., 2017), resulting in DNA condensation by forming large DNA loops.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data, the proposed model in Figure 7, and a citation to prior work (Fisher et al., 2017).

claim: CTP hydrolysis might be a means to recover ParB dimers from the DNA.
source: CTP hydrolysis might be a means to recover ParB dimers from the DNA (black arrow).
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on the proposed model in Figure 7.

claim: Protein roadblocks constrain diffusion of ParB proteins.
source: Protein roadblocks constrain diffusion of ParB proteins (red arrow).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2 and the proposed model in Figure 7.

claim: MT experiments including EcoRI roadblocks directly linked ParB diffusion with condensation because the DNA region non-accessible to ParB, due to EcoRI blocking, remained non-condensed.
source: Importantly, MT experiments including EcoRI roadblocks directly linked ParB diffusion with condensation because the DNA region non-accessible to ParB, due to EcoRI blocking, remained non-condensed (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The molecular basis for the protein-protein interactions that hold the ParB network together remains unclear.
source: The molecular basis for the protein-protein interactions that hold the ParB network together in our model remains unclear and is an important subject for future study.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Disruption of CTD-CTD interactions decondenses DNA in vitro and prevents the formation of ParB networks in vivo.
source: For example, we have previously provided direct evidence that disruption of CTD-CTD interactions decondenses DNA in vitro and prevents the formation of ParB networks in vivo, so these protein-protein interactions may contribute to network formation (Figure 7, step 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' prior work.

claim: CTD-CTD interactions may be important for closing the sliding clamp around DNA.
source: However, we note that our results can also be re-interpreted in the light of the new concept of topological engagement between DNA and a ParB toroidal clamp. If CTD-CTD interactions are important for closing the sliding clamp around DNA as has been suggested (Jalal et al., 2020; Soh et al., 2019), then disruption of these interactions would dissolve ParB networks, not by breaking protein-protein interactions between ParB molecules, but rather by releasing the constrained DNA loops and promoting ParB dissociation into free solution.
